mainTopic: A gift to an heir 'and after you, to so-and-so'; the משנה and גמרא on giving one's property away from one's sons
overview: The amud opens by finishing a court case. A man gave his property to someone who was also his heir, 'and after you, to so-and-so.' רב עיליש wanted to give the second person a share, but רבא rejected this as mere compromise, pointing to the ruling of רב אחא בר רב עויא, and a פסוק was read to comfort the embarrassed רב עיליש. Then a new משנה teaches that giving all one's property to others and leaving out one's sons is valid, but the חכמים are not pleased. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says that if the sons behave badly, the father is remembered for good. The גמרא asks whether the חכמים disagree with him. It first tries to answer from the story of יוסף בן יועזר and the pearl, but the two versions of the treasurers' record contradict each other, so nothing is proven. שמואל's teaching then gives the answer: never take part in moving an inheritance, even from a bad son to a good son. Finally, a ברייתא tells how יונתן בן עוזיאל received a man's property, gave a third back to the sons, and defended himself when שמאי came to protest. His defense continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A real case: property given to an heir, and after him to someone else
steps.stepSummary: A man gave his property to someone who was fit to inherit him, adding 'and after you, to so-and-so.' The first receiver died, and the second came to claim the property.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a man who told another person: 'My property is yours, and after you it goes to so-and-so.' The first person was someone who would have inherited him anyway. The first person died, and the second person came to claim the property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real case that came to court. It is setting up the question of whether the second person gets anything.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key detail is that the first receiver was also a natural heir of the giver. That makes the first receiver look like an heir, not just someone who got a gift. The next steps argue about what that means for the second person.

keyTerms.meaning: My property is yours, and after you, to so-and-so (a gift with a 'next in line')
The second receiver, the one 'after you'
Fit to inherit him, a natural heir

phrases.english: There was a certain man who said to his fellow:
"My property is yours, and after you, to so-and-so,"
and the first one was fit to inherit from him.
The first one died,
and the second came and was claiming the property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a court-case story that continues the earlier discussion on this דף about 'after you, to so-and-so' when the first receiver is an heir.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Lays out the facts: an heir received the property first, and after his death a second person named in the gift claims it.

steps.title: רב עיליש thinks the second person also takes a share
steps.stepSummary: רב עיליש, sitting before רבא, was about to rule that the second person also gets part of the property.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב עיליש, sitting in front of רבא, thought he would rule: the second person also takes a share.
steps.whatsHappening: רב עיליש offers his first idea for how to rule in the case. This idea is about to be rejected.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'also' tells us he did not want to give everything to the second person. He wanted to split it, so the second person shares with the first person's heirs. This is a middle-ground ruling, and that is exactly what רבא attacks next.

keyTerms.meaning: He thought, he was inclined to

phrases.aramaic: סְבַר רַב עִילִישׁ קַמֵּיהּ דְּרָבָא לְמֵימַר:
phrases.english: Rav Ilish, sitting before Rava, thought to say:
The second one also takes.
phrases.notes: "Also" means he shares the property together with the first one's heirs, not that he takes it all.

steps.triggerLanguage: סְבַר רַב עִילִישׁ קַמֵּיהּ דְּרָבָא לְמֵימַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a proposed ruling for the case described in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A first suggestion that is later rejected: the second receiver shares the property with the first receiver's heirs.

steps.title: רבא rejects the split ruling and points to רב אחא בר רב עויא
steps.stepSummary: רבא says that splitting the property is how 'compromise judges' rule. He reminds רב עיליש that this exact case was already decided by רב אחא בר רב עויא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: That is how judges who just split everything rule! Isn't this exactly the case that רב אחא בר רב עויא sent a ruling about?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא shoots down רב עיליש's idea. He calls it lazy splitting and shows that an earlier ruling already covers this case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא makes two points. First, splitting the property is not real judging; it just avoids deciding. Second, the case is the same as the one רב אחא בר רב עויא ruled on earlier on this דף, where the second person got nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: Judges who split the difference, compromise judges
Sent (a ruling, by letter or messenger)

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not saying the second person gets everything. He is saying the second person gets nothing, just like in the earlier ruling.

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: This is רבא speaking to רב עיליש.

phrases.english: Judges of compromise judge this way!
phrases.notes: He means judges who just cut everything down the middle instead of really deciding who is right.

phrases.aramaic: לָאו הַיְינוּ דִּשְׁלַח רַב אַחָא בַּר רַב עַוְיָא?
phrases.english: Isn't this the very case that Rav Aḥa bar Rav Avya sent a ruling about?
phrases.notes: This points back to the ruling quoted earlier on this דף, where the second person got nothing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רב עיליש's proposed ruling from step 2.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the whole idea that the second receiver gets any share.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The split ruling is only a compromise, and it goes against the earlier ruling of רב אחא בר רב עויא on this exact case.
steps.whatToRemember: When the first receiver is a natural heir, the second person named 'after you' does not get a share. רבא follows the ruling of רב אחא בר רב עויא.

steps.title: רב עיליש is embarrassed and a פסוק is read about him
steps.stepSummary: רב עיליש felt ashamed of his mistake. The פסוק 'I, ה׳, will hasten it in its time' was read about him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב עיליש was embarrassed. The פסוק was read about him: 'I, ה׳, will hasten it in its time.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends. רב עיליש feels bad about his mistake, and a פסוק is quoted about what happened.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק is read to comfort him. The idea is that ה׳ arranged for the mistake to be caught just in time, before a wrong ruling was carried out. So the story closes with the correct ruling standing and the error fixed.

keyTerms.meaning: I will hasten it in its time

phrases.english: He was embarrassed.
phrases.notes: This is רב עיליש, upset that he almost ruled wrongly.

phrases.english: He read about him:
"I, the Lord, will hasten it in its time."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the story after רבא's correction in step 3.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The mistaken split ruling was stopped in time; the correct ruling (the second person gets nothing) stands.

steps.title: New משנה: giving all your property to others and leaving your sons out
steps.stepSummary: If someone writes his property over to others and leaves his sons with nothing, the gift works, but the חכמים are not pleased with him.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If a person writes his property over to others and leaves his sons out, what he did is valid, but the חכמים are not happy with him.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It rules that a gift that skips the sons is legally valid but frowned upon.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה separates two things: the law and the attitude. Legally, a person may give his property to whoever he wants while alive, so the gift stands. But the חכמים dislike it, because it takes away the inheritance his sons would have received.

keyTerms.meaning: One who writes over his property (as a gift in a document)
What he did is done (it is valid)
The חכמים are not pleased with him

steps.confusionAlert: 'The חכמים are not pleased' does not cancel the gift. The gift fully works; it is only disapproved of.

phrases.english: Mishnah:
One who writes his property over to others
and left his sons out –
what he did is done,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אֵין רוּחַ חֲכָמִים נוֹחָה הֵימֶנּוּ.
phrases.english: but the spirit of the Sages is not pleased with him.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַכּוֹתֵב אֶת נְכָסָיו לַאֲחֵרִים וְהִנִּיחַ אֶת בָּנָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה, unrelated to the story that just ended.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A gift of all one's property to others, leaving out the sons, is valid, but the חכמים disapprove.
steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches that something can be fully allowed by law and still not be the right thing to do.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: if the sons behaved badly, the father is praised
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says that if the sons were not acting properly, the father who gave his property to others is remembered for good.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: If his sons were not behaving properly, he is remembered for good.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל adds a case where skipping the sons is actually praised.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first part of the משנה said the חכמים are unhappy with such a gift. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says this changes when the sons are behaving badly. Then keeping the money away from them is a good deed, and the father is praised.

keyTerms.meaning: Behaving properly, acting the right way

steps.whatToRemember: The gift that skips the sons is always valid. The only question is whether it is frowned upon (normally) or praised (when the sons behave badly, according to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל).

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:

phrases.aramaic: אִם לֹא הָיוּ בָּנָיו נוֹהֲגִים כַּשּׁוּרָה –
phrases.english: If his sons were not behaving properly –
he is remembered for good.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds an exception to the disapproval stated in step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the sons are not behaving properly, giving the property to others is praiseworthy.

steps.title: Do the רבנן disagree with רבן שמעון בן גמליאל?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the חכמים disagree with רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who said that giving property away from sons who do not act properly is praiseworthy.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: They asked: do the רבנן disagree with רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins discussing the משנה by asking a question. Did the first, unnamed opinion (the חכמים) disagree with רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, or does everyone agree with him?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first, unnamed opinion in the משנה said the חכמים are not pleased with someone who writes his property away from his sons. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל added that if the sons were not acting properly, the father is remembered for good. The question is whether the first opinion is displeased even when the sons are bad, which would mean they argue, or only when the sons are good, which would mean they agree.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was raised before them, used for a real open question
The Rabbis, meaning the first, unnamed opinion in the משנה

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two opinions. 'רבנן' here is the first, unnamed opinion in the משנה (Step 5), not רבן שמעון בן גמליאל (Step 6).

phrases.english: Gemara
A question was asked before them:
Do the Rabbis disagree
with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel,
phrases.notes: This refers back to his ruling about sons who were not acting properly (Step 6).

phrases.english: or not?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ: מִי פְּלִיגִי רַבָּנַן עֲלֵיהּ דְּרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל, אוֹ לָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא's discussion of the two opinions in the משנה (Steps 5 and 6).
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Are the חכמים displeased even when the sons are not acting properly, which would mean they disagree with רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, or do they agree with him?

steps.title: יוסף בן יועזר dedicates his money, and his son finds a pearl
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a story to answer the question. יוסף בן יועזר dedicated his money to the בית המקדש because his son did not act properly. Later the son found a pearl inside a fish.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: יוסף בן יועזר had a son who did not act properly. He had a vessel full of dinars, and he dedicated it to the Temple. The son went and married the daughter of King ינאי's crown weaver. When his wife gave birth, he bought her a fish. He cut it open and found a pearl inside.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says 'come and hear' and starts a story that will help answer the question. This step only sets up the story; its point comes later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יוסף בן יועזר, a great and righteous sage, kept his property away from his son who did not act properly by dedicating it to הקדש. This is exactly the kind of case רבן שמעון בן גמליאל was talking about. The rest of the story will show how this act was viewed.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear, which introduces a source brought as a proof
He dedicated it to the בית המקדש (הקדש)

phrases.english: Come and hear:

phrases.aramaic: דְּיוֹסֵף בֶּן יוֹעֶזֶר הָיָה לוֹ בֵּן
phrases.english: For Yosef ben Yo'ezer had a son
who was not acting properly.
He had a vessel full of dinars;
he got up and dedicated it.
The son went and married the daughter of the crown weaver
of King Yannai.
His wife gave birth;
he bought her a fish.
He tore it open and found a pearl in it.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: דְּיוֹסֵף בֶּן יוֹעֶזֶר הָיָה לוֹ בֵּן שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה נוֹהֵג כַּשּׁוּרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a story brought to answer the question in Step 7.
steps.raayaObject: Whether the חכמים agree that keeping property from a son who does not act properly is praiseworthy.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of יוסף בן יועזר dedicating his coins to the בית המקדש because of his son.

steps.title: The wife advises bringing the pearl to the Temple treasurers
steps.stepSummary: The son's wife tells him not to sell the pearl to the king, who would pay too little. He should go to the Temple treasurers and let them set the price himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: She said to him: Don't bring it to the king, because they will take it from you for a low price. Go bring it to the Temple treasurers. And don't set its price yourself, because promising something to the Temple is like handing it over to an ordinary person. Let them set the price.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. The wife gives her husband smart advice about where to sell the pearl and how to avoid losing money on it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A promise to הקדש is binding right away, just as a completed handover is binding between ordinary people. If the son named a price too low, he could not take it back. So he should let the treasurers name a fair price.

keyTerms.meaning: The treasurers of the בית המקדש
A person's verbal promise to the בית המקדש is as binding as actually handing something over to an ordinary person

steps.whyThisMatters: This line includes the well-known halachic rule אמירתו לגבוה כמסירתו להדיוט: words alone are enough to obligate a person to הקדש.

phrases.english: She said to him:
Do not bring it to the king,
for they will take it from you for a small price;
go bring it to the treasurers.
And do not set its price yourself,
for a person's promise to the Most High
is like his handing something over to an ordinary person,
phrases.notes: She means that if he names a low price, he is stuck with it and cannot back out.

phrases.english: rather, let them set its price.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story from Step 8 with the wife's advice about the pearl.
steps.raayaObject: Whether the חכמים agree that keeping property from a son who does not act properly is praiseworthy.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The continuing story of יוסף בן יועזר's son.

steps.title: The pearl is valued at thirteen, and the son dedicates six
steps.stepSummary: The treasurers valued the pearl at thirteen vessels of dinars but had only seven to pay. The son took seven and dedicated the remaining six to Heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: He brought it, and they valued it at thirteen vessels of dinars. They told him: We have seven; we don't have six. He said to them: Give me seven, and the six are hereby dedicated to Heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. The pearl turns out to be worth thirteen vessels of coins, and the son generously gives the part the treasury cannot pay to the בית המקדש. The lesson of the story comes after this section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The father had dedicated one vessel of coins, keeping it from his son. Now the son receives seven vessels from the בית המקדש's treasury and gives six more to it. This sets up the story's ending, which will show how the father's act turned out and so answer the question in Step 7.

keyTerms.meaning: Dedicated to Heaven, meaning given to the בית המקדש

steps.confusionAlert: The story is not finished here. The attempted proof for the question in Step 7 comes from the ending, in steps 11 through 14.

phrases.english: He brought it;
they valued it at thirteen vessels of dinars.
They said to him:
Seven there are; six there are not.
phrases.notes: The treasury had only seven vessels of coins on hand to pay him.

phrases.english: He said to them:
Give me seven;
the six are hereby dedicated to Heaven.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story from Step 9: the pearl is valued, and the son dedicates the unpaid six to Heaven.
steps.raayaObject: Whether the חכמים agree that keeping property from a son who does not act properly is praiseworthy.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The continuing story of יוסף בן יועזר's son, whose ending comes next.

steps.title: What the treasurers wrote: two versions
steps.stepSummary: The treasurers recorded the event. One version praises the son for bringing in six. Another version says he took out seven.
steps.simpleTranslation: The treasurers wrote: 'יוסף בן יועזר brought in one, and his son brought in six.' Some say they wrote: 'יוסף בן יועזר brought in one, and his son took out seven.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story of the pearl ends with a record the Temple treasurers wrote down. The גמרא gives two different versions of what that record said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, the son is praised: he added six to the הקדש. In the second version, he is described as taking seven out of the הקדש. The difference matters, because the next step tries to learn from this wording.

keyTerms.meaning: Brought in (gave to the Temple treasury)
Took out (removed from the Temple treasury)
And some say (introduces a second version)

phrases.english: They arose and wrote:
phrases.notes: "They" means the Temple treasurers from the story.

phrases.english: Yosef ben Yo'ezer brought in one,
and his son brought in six.
phrases.notes: These are the six he gave back to Heaven in step 10.

phrases.english: And there are those who say:
Yosef ben Yo'ezer brought in one,
and his son took out seven.
phrases.notes: These are the seven he was paid for the pearl.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the story begun in step 8 with the treasurers' written record.
steps.raayaObject: Whether the חכמים agree that giving property away from improper sons is good
steps.raayaSupportSource: The wording of the treasurers' record in the יוסף בן יועזר story

steps.title: Inference: 'brought in' shows he acted well
steps.stepSummary: Since the record says the son 'brought in', יוסף בן יועזר must have acted well.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since they said 'brought in', it follows that he acted well!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to learn from the first version. The positive word 'brought in' suggests the whole move was a good thing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the treasurers described the result as a gain for the הקדש, then יוסף בן יועזר's choice to give away his money instead of leaving it to his son was praiseworthy. That would mean the חכמים agree with רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.

phrases.english: From the fact that they said "brought in,"
it follows that he acted well!
phrases.notes: "He" is יוסף בן יועזר, who gave his money away instead of leaving it to his son.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִדְּקָא אָמְרִי הִכְנִיס מִכְּלָל דְּשַׁפִּיר עֲבַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a conclusion from the first version of the record in step 11.
steps.raayaObject: That giving property away from improper sons is good
steps.raayaSupportSource: The word הִכְנִיס in the first version

steps.title: On the contrary: 'took out' shows he did not act well
steps.stepSummary: The second version says 'took out', which suggests the opposite: he did not act well.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the contrary! Since they said 'took out', it follows that he did not act well!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back using the second version. The word 'took out' sounds negative, so it points the other way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the second version, the son is seen as removing seven from the הקדש. Because the father cut him off, the son ended up taking money out of the Temple treasury, so the father's move looks bad. The same story now proves the opposite.

phrases.english: On the contrary, from the fact that they said "took out,"
it follows that he did not act well!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the proof of step 12 around by using the other version.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof drawn from the word הִכְנִיס
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The other version uses הוֹצִיא, which implies the opposite conclusion

steps.title: No proof can be learned from this story
steps.stepSummary: Since the two versions point in opposite directions, nothing can be learned from the story.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, nothing can be learned from this.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the proof completely. The story cannot answer the question from step 7.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One version supports giving property away, and the other opposes it. Since we do not know which wording is correct, the story proves nothing either way. The גמרא looks for another answer, which step 16 gives.

keyTerms.meaning: There is nothing to learn from it

steps.whatToRemember: The יוסף בן יועזר story does not settle whether the חכמים agree with רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, because its two versions contradict each other.

phrases.english: Rather, from this there is nothing to learn.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the back-and-forth of steps 12 and 13 with no result.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The story cannot serve as a proof for either side.

steps.title: So what is the final ruling?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the conclusion is on this question.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the conclusion about it?
steps.whatsHappening: Since the story proved nothing, the גמרא asks again for the final answer. This line sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question from step 7 still needs an answer: is it right to move property away from sons who do not act properly? The גמרא now looks for a clear ruling, and the next step gives it.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the conclusion about it?

phrases.english: What is the conclusion about it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Since the story in step 14 proved nothing, the גמרא asks for a final ruling, which step 16 supplies.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical ruling on moving an inheritance away from improper sons

steps.title: שמואל: never take part in moving an inheritance
steps.stepSummary: שמואל told רב יהודה not to be present when an inheritance is moved away, even from a bad son to a good son, and certainly not from a son to a daughter.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: שמואל said to רב יהודה, 'Sharp one, do not be where an inheritance is transferred, even from a bad son to a good son, and all the more so from a son to a daughter.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a teaching of שמואל. He tells his student not even to be present when someone moves an inheritance away from the proper heir.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even when the heir is a bad son and the new receiver is a good son, it is still wrong to change the inheritance. Moving it from a son to a daughter, who does not inherit by Torah law when there are sons, is even worse. So the ruling does not follow the praise of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.

keyTerms.meaning: Transferring an inheritance away from the heir

steps.whatToRemember: The ruling: do not move an inheritance away from the proper heir, even from a bad son to a good son.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the practical ruling of the סוגיא: even a son who behaves badly should not be cut out of his inheritance.

phrases.english: Come and hear,
as Shmuel said to Rav Yehuda:

phrases.aramaic: שִׁינָּנָא, לָא תְּיהַוֵּי בֵּי עַבּוֹרֵי אַחְסָנְתָּא;
phrases.english: Sharp one, do not be present where an inheritance is transferred;
phrases.notes: שִׁינָּנָא is a nickname שמואל used for his student רב יהודה.

phrases.english: even from a bad son to a good son,
and all the more so from a son to a daughter.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ שְׁמוּאֵל לְרַב יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question asked in step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: One should not take part in moving an inheritance away from an heir, even from a bad son to a good son.

steps.title: A man gives his property to יונתן בן עוזיאל
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא tells of a man whose sons did not act properly, so he wrote his property over to יונתן בן עוזיאל.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: There was a case of a man whose sons did not act properly. He went and wrote his property over to יונתן בן עוזיאל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new ברייתא with another story about a man who gave his property away from his sons. This step sets up the case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same kind of situation as רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's case: sons who do not behave properly, and a father who gives his property to someone else. The receiver here is a great Sage, יונתן בן עוזיאל.

phrases.english: The Sages taught: There was an incident with one man
whose sons did not act properly,
he arose and wrote his property over
to Yonatan ben Uzziel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new ברייתא about the same kind of case as step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A man with improper sons wrote all his property to יונתן בן עוזיאל.

steps.title: יונתן בן עוזיאל splits the property into three
steps.stepSummary: יונתן בן עוזיאל sold a third, dedicated a third, and gave a third back to the man's sons.
steps.simpleTranslation: What did יונתן בן עוזיאל do? He sold a third, dedicated a third to the Temple, and returned a third to the man's sons.
steps.whatsHappening: The story tells what יונתן בן עוזיאל did with the property he received. He divided it into three parts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He did not keep everything for himself. One third he sold, one third he gave to הקדש, and one third he gave back to the sons, even though the father had wanted them cut out. The story continues after this point.

phrases.english: What did Yonatan ben Uzziel do?
He sold a third, and consecrated a third,
and returned a third to his sons.
phrases.notes: "His sons" means the sons of the man who gave the property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story from step 17 by telling what the receiver did.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: יונתן בן עוזיאל divided the property: one third sold, one third dedicated, one third returned to the sons.

steps.title: שמאי comes to protest
steps.stepSummary: שמאי comes to יונתן בן עוזיאל with his staff and traveling bag to protest the return of property to the sons.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמאי came to him with his staff and his traveling bag.
steps.whatsHappening: שמאי shows up to object to what יונתן בן עוזיאל did. This line sets up the defense that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The father wanted his property kept away from his sons, but יונתן בן עוזיאל gave a third of it back to them. שמאי's visit is a silent challenge: you went against the father's wishes. The words of the protest are not quoted; his arrival is the objection.

keyTerms.meaning: The great תנא, leader of בית שמאי

phrases.english: Shammai came to him
phrases.notes: "Him" is יונתן בן עוזיאל, from the story in the step just before this one.

phrases.english: with his staff and his traveling bag.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Objects to the last action in Step 18, giving a third back to the sons.
steps.kashyaTarget: יונתן בן עוזיאל's returning a third of the property to the sons
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The father deliberately kept the property from his sons, so giving it back to them seems to go against his wishes.

steps.title: Returning to the sons is as final as selling or dedicating
steps.stepSummary: יונתן בן עוזיאל answers that if שמאי can undo the sale and the הקדש, he can also undo the return to the sons.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: שמאי, if you can take back what I sold and what I dedicated, then you can take back what I returned.
steps.whatsHappening: יונתן בן עוזיאל begins defending himself. He says the third he gave back is just as fixed as the other two thirds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The property became fully his, so all three things he did with it are equal acts of an owner. No one would say a sale to a buyer or a gift to הקדש can be undone. So the gift back to the sons cannot be undone either. His sentence keeps going after this point.

keyTerms.meaning: To take back, to take away from someone
That I dedicated (to the בית המקדש)

steps.confusionAlert: יונתן בן עוזיאל is not saying שמאי really can undo the sale or the הקדש. He means: just as you cannot undo those, you cannot undo what I returned.

phrases.english: He said to him: Shammai,
if you are able to take back
what I sold
and what I dedicated,
you can take back what I returned;

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: שַׁמַּאי, אִם אַתָּה יָכוֹל לְהוֹצִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers שמאי's silent protest from Step 19.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Comparison: all three acts are equal acts of a full owner.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Giving the property back to the sons goes against the father's wishes and should be undone.
steps.terutzMaskana: The return to the sons is as final as the sale and the הקדש, which nobody can undo.
